personality_voice.book_baseline: Karkaroff in the books is defined by a layered, contradictory personality built from observable patterns across many scenes. His dominant register is unctuous flattery — 'How are you, my dear fellow' (Scene 4), his 'fruity, unctuous voice' (Scene 5) — but this surface warmth is consistently undercut by cold eyes that 'did not extend to his smile' (Scene 7) and 'remained cold and shrewd.' He is selectively warm: fawning over Viktor with offers of mulled wine, then snapping viciously at Poliakoff in the same breath — 'I wasn't offering it to you, Poliakoff... disgusting boy' (Scene 21). His voice shifts register depending on audience: unctuous with Dumbledore and judges ('you are our objective judges,' Scene 50), cold and steely when threatened ('his steely smile... his blue eyes were like chips of ice,' Scene 43), explosive when cornered ('in which Durmstrang will most certainly not be competing!' Scene 57), and barely controlled when frightened — his hands 'had balled themselves into fists' despite his attempt to sound disdainful (Scene 61). At his trial, even chained and terrified, the 'familiar unctuous note' in his voice persists (Scene 214). He is petty (twirling his goatee for photographs, Scene 84), vindictive (giving Harry a 4 during the first task, Scene 119), and capable of real cowardice — he fleeing at the end without a word. His speech patterns include rhetorical flourish ('Are we not right to be proud...,' Scene 131), abrupt hostility, and anxious repetition ('I have more!... No, no, no,' trial scenes). He is not a simple villain but a self-serving opportunist whose fear drives every action.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves several surface elements of Karkaroff's personality: the unctuous greeting to Dumbledore ('Albus' / 'Igor'), the cold competitive edge in the champions' chamber ('You seem to have given this a fair bit of thought, Mad-Eye,' Film Scene 4), the booming public support for Krum ('Come on! Krum! Krum! Krum!' Film Scene 8), and the trial scenes where the unctuous, desperate quality — 'No, no, no... I have more!' — is directly rendered (Film Scene 6). The selective favouritism toward Krum is visible in the arrival scene. His cowardice and fear are implied by Sirius's warning ('no one stops being a Death Eater,' Film Scene 5) and Moody's later confirmation of his flight (referenced in passing). However, the film loses his most revealing personality moments: the vicious snap at Poliakoff (cut — this scene is absent from film corpus), the moment his fists betray his fear during the Moody confrontation (no equivalent in film), the goatee-twirling nervous habit observed multiple times, his livid explosion at Krum's attack ('Treachery! It is a plot!'), his spitting at Dumbledore's feet, and his sustained rhetorical self-justification in the Yule Ball gardens scene (cut as non-theatrical). The film reduces him to two modes — cold competitor and desperate informant — without the texture of his cowardly self-preservation instinct expressed through small observable behaviors.
personality_voice.difference: The unctuous-yet-cold duality is partially preserved in the trial and champions' chamber. But the film removes: (1) the snap at Poliakoff showing his selective cruelty; (2) the physically observable signs of concealed fear (balled fists, burning face); (3) the rhetorical self-aggrandizement at the Yule Ball (non-theatrical); (4) the spectacular explosion and spitting at Dumbledore after Krum is attacked; (5) the nervous goatee-twirling as a repeated behavioral tell. The film Karkaroff is recognizable but stripped of the contradictory micro-behaviors that give him his book texture.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The character remains recognizable — unctuous, cold, competitive, cowardly — so no severe penalty applies. But several important behavioral patterns and contradictions (the Poliakoff snap, the physical fear tells, the Krum-attack explosion) are absent, and the voice is simplified to two modes rather than the multi-register book version. This warrants a score in the 14–17 range: recognizable but with reduced contradictions and tonal range.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Karkaroff serves multiple active narrative functions in the books. (1) He is an active threat and suspect: Harry and Sirius spend significant time assessing whether he put Harry's name in the goblet; he spies on the first task in the forest at night (Scene 88–90); he gives Harry a biased score of 4 in the first task (Scene 119); he is the only judge not showing relief after Harry's second-task success (Scene 154). (2) He is the primary vehicle through which Voldemort's returning power is first concretely signaled to the reader: he shows Snape his darkening Dark Mark in Potions class (Scenes 170–178), and Snape's pensieve memory confirms both their Marks are burning (Scene 283). This moment is a key plot-and-thematic beat — the first physical proof of Voldemort's return visible to characters other than Harry. (3) He confronts and threatens in the champions' chamber (Scene 43–57), filing formal protests and demanding the goblet be reset. (4) His trial in the pensieve is a major exposition scene that reveals the Death Eater network and introduces Barty Crouch Jr. (5) His flight confirms Voldemort's return to the reader and to the characters at the end of Book 4. (6) He is used by Dumbledore in HBP (Scene 283–286) as a foil for Snape's courage.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves: the champions' chamber protest (reduced in force); the trial scene which retains his informant role and his naming of Barty Crouch Jr. (a key plot function); his arrival and competitive presence; Sirius's warning about him as a Death Eater (Film Scene 5); the brief Snape corridor scene (Film Scene 7, though the arm-showing is off-screen and the scene is minimal). The film loses: his active nighttime spying on the first task (absent from film corpus); his biased score of 4 in the first task (absent — no scoring tableau shown in film); his pointed refusal to look relieved after the second task (absent); the full Potions classroom scene where he hovers for a double period, deliberately prevents Snape from leaving, and explicitly shows the Dark Mark (cut as non-theatrical). His flight is mentioned by Moody in the book denouement but is not dramatized or specifically confirmed in the theatrical film. His role as the primary signal of Voldemort's return through the Dark Mark is transferred or collapsed: the film's corridor scene (Film Scene 7) shows him opening his sleeve briefly but this is handled without the extended tension or Harry's active eavesdropping that makes it structurally meaningful.
narrative_role_agency.difference: The spying on the first task (active agency) is removed. The biased first-task score (active antagonism/agency) is removed. The extended Potions classroom scene where Karkaroff actively pursues Snape and demonstrates the Mark is non-theatrical (cut). His role as the primary in-story signal of Voldemort's return through the Dark Mark is substantially reduced. The trial scene retains his informant agency and the Barty Jr. reveal. The champions' chamber protest is retained but compressed. Overall, his active antagonist and plot-driver functions are significantly curtailed.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Several of Karkaroff's active narrative functions — spying, biased scoring, the sustained Snape pursuit in Potions, the Mark revelation as a structural plot beat — are removed or heavily reduced. The trial scene retains meaningful agency (naming Barty Jr. is structurally important). His role as a suspect/threat is conveyed mainly through Sirius's dialogue rather than through his own actions. This is a clear reduction of both role and agency, warranting a score of 10–13.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Karkaroff's motivations are unusually consistent and clear across all his appearances: self-preservation above all else. Every action traces back to this. He named Death Eaters in court to escape Azkaban, calculating which names had already been caught (his visible panic when Dolohov and Rosier are already apprehended, Scenes 233–239). He competes viciously in the Tournament to win prestige and beat Dumbledore, feeding Viktor information about the first task (Scene 116). He gives Harry a 4 to damage his standing. He pursues Snape anxiously because he needs reassurance about the Dark Mark — he is afraid of what its darkening means, and specifically afraid of retribution from Voldemort if he returns (Scenes 140, 163–178, 283). His internal conflict is between his desire to appear loyal/respectable (as Durmstrang headmaster, as someone who 'turned his life around') and his deep cowardice and self-interest. When the Mark burns, he flees — consistent with every prior choice. He has no genuine moral conviction; his 'remorse' at the trial is performative and calculated.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The trial scene preserves his core motivation well: the desperation to escape Azkaban, the calculating way he offers names, the visible panic when his names are already known ('Dead?! I didn't know'), and the shift to naming Barty Jr. as a last resort are all present in Film Scene 6. Sirius's line in Film Scene 5 — 'no one stops being a Death Eater' — frames his motivation as ongoing self-interest rather than genuine reform. The corridor scene (Film Scene 7) shows him anxious and consulting Snape, preserving the fear-of-retribution motivation. However, the film does not develop his calculated self-interest across multiple scenes the way the books do — the biased scoring, the nighttime spying, the sustained pursuit of Snape in Potions. The motivation is present but underexplained across the narrative, relying heavily on a single Sirius exposition line.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The core motivation (self-preservation, fear of Voldemort's return) is present and correctly rendered in both the trial and the corridor scene. The film compresses rather than changes his motivations. The main loss is that the film does not dramatize his motivation playing out in active choices across multiple scenes — it tells rather than shows.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified and underexplained but not fundamentally changed. The self-preservation drive is intact and observable in the trial scene and in Sirius's framing. Compression is the main issue, not alteration. This falls in the 8–10 range: partially altered through flattening, not through distortion.

character_arc.book_baseline: Karkaroff's arc in GoF is a complete, internally logical coward's trajectory: (1) Arrival — performatively warm, competitive, calculating; (2) Escalating anxiety — the Dark Mark darkens, he pursues Snape obsessively, his fear grows visibly through the year; (3) Explosion — he accuses Dumbledore of treachery after Krum is attacked, spits at Dumbledore's feet; (4) Flight — he abandons his school and his champion the night Voldemort returns; (5) Death — confirmed in HBP, killed by Voldemort within a year. This arc is also retroactively illuminated by the pensieve trial: we see who he was before Azkaban (ruthless, calculating, self-serving under the Death Eaters), which makes his later anxious self-preservation legible as continuous character. Dumbledore's contrast in HBP ('You are a braver man by far than Igor Karkaroff,' Scene 286) serves as a retrospective capstone, using his arc to define Snape's courage by contrast. The arc is not one of redemption or growth — it is a sustained, revealed cowardice.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film captures the beginning (competitive arrival, unctuous warmth) and the trial-era Karkaroff (calculating informant). The escalating anxiety arc during the year — the sustained Snape pursuit, the Potions classroom confrontation — is lost because that scene is non-theatrical. The explosion at Krum's attack ('Treachery! It is a plot!') and the spitting at Dumbledore are absent from the film corpus. His flight is confirmed verbally by Moody in the book denouement but the film's equivalent confirmation is not clearly present in the theatrical film corpus provided. The HBP contrast with Snape (Scene 283–286) has no film equivalent — this entire scene is absent from the film corpus. The arc's middle and end sections — the visible disintegration of composure through fear, the explosion, the flight, the death — are largely absent or unconfirmed.
character_arc.difference: The film has the arc's starting point (arrival, calculated warmth) and one major early beat (the trial). The escalating fear across the year, the explosion/breakdown, the flight, and the retrospective capstone in HBP are all absent or unconfirmed. The arc is present only in its first quarter.
character_arc.penalty_logic: This is more than compression — the arc's turning points (anxiety-to-explosion-to-flight) are missing, not just shortened. The audience cannot track his disintegration across the year. The HBP retrospective is entirely absent. This warrants a score of 8–10: arc is incomplete and missing important steps.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Karkaroff has two defining relationships in the books. (1) Karkaroff and Snape: This is the most important relationship for his characterization. They share a past as Death Eaters; Karkaroff tried to name Snape at his trial (Scene 250). During GoF, Karkaroff seeks Snape out anxiously, needing reassurance, treating Snape as his only peer who understands his fear. Snape is contemptuous and avoidant — 'Then flee. I will make your excuses. I, however, am remaining at Hogwarts' (Scene 141). The dynamic is one of Karkaroff's desperate dependence versus Snape's cold superiority. This relationship reveals Karkaroff's cowardice (he needs someone else to tell him what to do) and Snape's courage by contrast. (2) Karkaroff and Krum: Selectively paternal — fawning over Krum as his asset while being contemptuous of other Durmstrang students. Karkaroff uses Krum instrumentally (he told him about the first task; his only visible emotional investment in the Tournament is through Krum). (3) Karkaroff and Dumbledore: Performative warmth masking deep rivalry and resentment — 'we are all protective of our private domains' (Scene 131). Karkaroff blames Dumbledore bitterly when things go wrong.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Karkaroff-Snape relationship in the film is reduced to a single brief corridor scene (Film Scene 7) where Karkaroff opens his sleeve and the two exchange a few words before Snape sees Harry and ends the scene. The anxious dependence, Snape's contemptuous 'Then flee,' and the sustained pursuit during Potions are all absent (the latter is non-theatrical). The Karkaroff-Krum relationship is shown only through surface moments: arrival together, Karkaroff cheering for Krum in the maze. The instrumental paternal quality exists but is not developed. The Karkaroff-Dumbledore relationship retains surface competitive tension in the champions' chamber but loses the Yule Ball conversational duel about secrets (non-theatrical) and the spitting incident.
key_relationships.difference: The Karkaroff-Snape relationship — the most characterization-rich relationship in the book — is reduced from a sustained, dramatically developed dynamic to a single wordless beat. The anxious-dependence/cold-contempt dynamic is not conveyed. Snape's defining 'I am not such a coward' line, which uses Karkaroff as a foil, is absent from the film (no HBP equivalent in corpus). The Krum relationship exists in outline only. The Dumbledore relationship loses its most revealing moments.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The Karkaroff-Snape dynamic is central to understanding both characters and is largely lost. The film audience cannot perceive Karkaroff's anxious dependence on Snape or the power imbalance that reveals his cowardice most clearly. This is a significant loss — it changes how the character is understood — warranting a score of 5–6.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Karkaroff in the books is a richly contradictory figure whose complexity operates on several levels: (1) The unctuous-yet-cruel contradiction, visible in the same scene (warm to Krum, vicious to Poliakoff); (2) The calculating coward who is still capable of genuine rage and explosion (the Krum attack scene); (3) The informant who tried to betray Snape in court but now desperately seeks his help — a relationship built on shared guilt and mutual calculation; (4) The performative reformer whose 'remorse so deep I can barely' is immediately undercut by his visible relief when his most useful names prove known; (5) The repeated behavioral tells — goatee-twirling as a nervous habit, fists balling under pressure — that give him physical specificity; (6) His function as thematic mirror: he represents the coward's path, against which Snape's choice to stay is measured (HBP). All of this creates a character who is petty, frightened, occasionally impressive in his cunning, and pathetic in his final flight.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film retains: the trial-scene desperation and calculating quality, the competitive cold presence in the champions' chamber, the surface unctuous warmth at arrival. It loses: the Poliakoff snap (selective cruelty), the goatee-twirling nervous habit, the physical fear tells (balled fists), the sustained Snape-pursuit anxiety (non-theatrical), the Krum-attack explosion and spitting, the Yule Ball conversational duel (non-theatrical), the HBP retrospective function, and the full arc of disintegration. The film Karkaroff is recognizable but has been reduced primarily to 'cold competitor' and 'desperate informant' — two of his facets, without the contradictions between them.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: Substantial. The contradictions that make him complex — warm/cruel, calculating/panicking, self-serving reformer/genuine coward — are only partially visible in the film. The material that would show his complexity across the Tournament year (the sustained anxiety, the explosion, the physical tells) is mostly absent. His thematic function as coward-foil to Snape is entirely absent.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The film preserves enough that he is not reduced to a single function, but the nuance, contradictions, and book-specific texture that make him more than a cold antagonist are largely gone. The absent material substantially changes the depth of the portrayal. Score in the 5–7 range: major flattening, character reduced to simpler functions.

score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (≤75): A core book function — the Dark Mark revelation scene in Potions, which is the primary in-story signal of Voldemort's return and the key beat of the Snape-Karkaroff dynamic — is absent (non-theatrical cut). This constitutes a transferred/lost structural beat of agency and function.

Cap 1 (≤85): The film removes major portions of Karkaroff's complexity, the sustained anxiety arc, key relationship dynamics, and the HBP thematic function. Even if remaining material were faithful, the overall cap applies.

Cap 5 (≤60): Karkaroff's arc and motivations are significantly underexplained across the film — the audience cannot track his disintegration through the year or understand his flight without the Potions and Yule Ball scenes. This cap is the binding constraint on the final score.
comparative.key_observations: The film's Karkaroff is a partial portrait: the trial scene is well-rendered and preserves his calculating desperation and the Barty Jr. revelation, and the champions' chamber protest retains his cold competitive quality. However, the theatrical cut loses or removes almost everything that happens between his arrival and the third task — the sustained anxiety arc, the defining Snape-Karkaroff dynamic in the Potions classroom, the Yule Ball argument, the biased scoring, the nighttime spying, and the explosion after Krum's attack. What remains is recognizable but thin: two facets (cold competitor, desperate informant) without the contradictions, behavioral texture, physical tells, or relational complexity that make him a rounded figure in the books. His most important narrative function — as the first in-story witness to Voldemort's Mark darkening, and as a cowardice-foil for Snape — is either cut or collapsed to a single brief shot. The score cap at 60 applies because his arc and motivations cannot be understood from the theatrical film alone, and Cap 3 applies because his primary agency beat (the Mark revelation) was transferred to a non-theatrical scene and is absent from the final film.
